title: Biomimicry: inventions copied from nature
playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if done at home today, with the materials listed. Fixes made. Leaves must be held by the stalk, because touching rubs off the wax (old or bruised leaves work less well, so pick a fresh one, and use an outer cabbage leaf if no arbi or lotus leaf can be found). The splash test counts wet spots on newspaper, because splash height is too hard to measure; the water must be 3 cm below the rim, and a beak that tumbles is dropped again from 20 cm. The ice test uses lidded cups and checks every 10 minutes. a bare cup's ice lasts about 20 to 40 minutes in strong sun. Wet cloth works less well on humid monsoon days. The Sock Walk works best from September to February and only on short weeds with a grown-up, because of snakes. Paperclip hooks must be small, and a grown-up bends them if the ends are sharp. Candle soot and the flame are grown-up steps, with a 2-minute cooling time. Cling film also holds partly by static, which the activity says honestly. Both games have rules for playing alone. Parents should know that the ice test needs about an hour, mostly waiting, so play the matching game in the shade meanwhile.

summary.text: This unit is about biomimicry. Biomimicry means copying a clever trick from a plant or an animal to solve a human problem. A burr's tiny hooks gave us Velcro. A lotus leaf's tiny waxy bumps gave us paint that washes itself clean in the rain. A kingfisher's beak gave Japan a quieter bullet train. Gecko toes, with millions of tiny hairs, gave us tape that grips without glue. Termite mounds gave builders ideas for buildings that stay cool. You will test these tricks at home, then design, build and test your own nature-inspired invention. Underneath it all are the same atoms and forces, and about 3.8 billion years of living things being tested.
summary.art: A child's notebook page: on the left a burr, a lotus leaf, a kingfisher, a gecko and a termite mound, and on the right, joined by dotted arrows, a Velcro strap, a raindrop rolling off a wall, a bullet train, a robot hand and a cool building.

intro.hook: Find a shoe, a bag or a watch with a Velcro strap. Pull it open slowly, close to your ear. Listen to that ripping sound. That sound was invented by a plant.
intro.text: In 1941, a Swiss engineer called George de Mestral came home from a walk in the mountains with his dog. Both of them were covered in prickly seed balls called burrs. Most people would just pick them off and grumble. George put one under a microscope instead. He saw hundreds of tiny hooks. Fourteen years later, he had a patent, an official paper that says an invention is yours. His invention was Velcro. What else are plants and animals hiding, if we look closely?
intro.art: A man in 1940s clothes bending over a microscope at a kitchen table, a burr on the glass slide, his dog beside him still covered in burrs.

outcomes: I can say what biomimicry is: copying a trick from a living thing to solve a human problem.
I can explain how a burr's hooks led to Velcro, and test what hooks hold on to best.
I can explain why a lotus leaf stays clean: tiny bumps and wax make water roll into balls that carry dirt away.
I can explain how a kingfisher's beak and a gecko's toes work, and what engineers made from them.
I can explain how a termite mound stays cool, and test which walls keep a model house coolest.
I can design, build and fairly test my own nature-inspired invention, record the results in a table and a bar chart, and improve it.
I can explain that these designs come from atoms pulling on each other and from billions of years of evolution. I can also say what scientists agree on and what they still argue about.

terms.meaning: Copying a trick from a plant or an animal to solve a human problem. 'Bio' means life. 'Mimic' means copy.
terms.example: Velcro copies the tiny hooks on a burr.
terms.art: A burr and a Velcro strap side by side, joined by a dotted arrow.

terms.meaning: A new thing, or a new way of doing something, that somebody thought up.
terms.example: The bicycle, the pressure cooker and Velcro are inventions.
terms.art: A light bulb above a child's head, and a pressure cooker, a bicycle and a Velcro strap below.

terms.meaning: A person who designs and builds things that solve problems, and tests them to see if they work.
terms.example: Engineers design bridges, trains, phones and water pumps.
terms.art: A woman engineer in a hard hat drawing a bridge, a small model bridge on her table.

terms.meaning: A plan for making something, drawn or written before you build it.
terms.example: A drawing of your invention with labels showing what each part does.
terms.art: A labelled pencil drawing of a backpack with arrows to its parts.

terms.meaning: A first, rough model of an invention, made to test if the idea works.
terms.example: A cardboard and paperclip fastener you make before a real one.
terms.art: A rough cardboard model held together with tape, next to a polished finished version.

terms.meaning: A test where you change only one thing and keep everything else the same. Then you know what caused the difference.
terms.example: Drop two dough shapes from the same height into the same bucket. Only the shape changes.
terms.art: Two identical buckets with two different dough shapes held at the same height above them.

terms.meaning: A seed or seed case covered in tiny hooks or spikes. It sticks to fur and clothes, so animals carry it to new places.
terms.example: After a walk through dry weeds, your socks can be full of prickly seeds.
terms.art: A round burr covered in hooked spines, stuck to a dog's fur.

terms.meaning: A way of joining two things. One side has tiny stiff hooks. The other side has tiny soft loops. The hooks catch in the loops.
terms.example: Velcro on school shoes and bags is hook and loop.
terms.art: A zoom into Velcro: stiff hooks on one side catching soft loops on the other.

terms.meaning: The way some leaves stay clean. Water rolls off in balls and carries the dirt away with it.
terms.example: After rain, lotus and arbi (colocasia) leaves have silver balls of water rolling on them, and look spotless.
terms.art: A lotus leaf with shiny round water drops, one drop rolling and picking up dust.

terms.meaning: A smooth, slippery stuff that water does not soak into. Many leaves make a thin layer of it on their skin.
terms.example: Candle wax, and the shiny coat on a cabbage leaf.
terms.art: A candle and a cabbage leaf, both with water drops beading up on them.

terms.meaning: When a surface makes water stay in round drops instead of spreading or soaking in.
terms.example: A raincoat is water-repelling. A paper towel is not. It soaks water up.
terms.art: A drop sitting round on a raincoat next to a drop soaking into a paper towel.

terms.meaning: Shaped so that air or water can flow smoothly around it. A streamlined thing is usually pointed at the front and smooth all over.
terms.example: Fish, dolphins, kingfishers and racing bicycles' helmets are streamlined.
terms.art: A fish, a kingfisher and a bullet train lined up, all with the same pointed shape.

terms.meaning: The push of air or water against something moving through it. Drag slows things down.
terms.example: Put your hand out of a moving bus window. The air pushing it back is drag.
terms.art: A hand out of a bus window with air arrows pushing it back.

terms.meaning: A loud bang when a fast train comes out of a tunnel. The train squeezes the air ahead of it inside the tunnel, and the squeezed air bursts out of the far end.
terms.example: Houses near tunnels in Japan were shaken by tunnel booms from early bullet trains.
terms.art: A tunnel in a hill with a burst of sound lines coming out of the far end before the train.

terms.meaning: A small lizard that can run up walls and walk upside down on ceilings. The house gecko, the chhipkali, lives in many Indian homes.
terms.example: A gecko waiting for insects near the tube light.
terms.art: A house gecko upside down on a ceiling near a tube light.

terms.meaning: The tiny hairs on a gecko's toes. Each one splits into hundreds of even tinier tips. Say it 'SEE-tee'.
terms.example: One gecko has millions of setae on its toes.
terms.art: A zoom from a gecko's toe to rows of hairs, to one hair splitting into a brush of tiny tips.

terms.meaning: A tall tower of mud that termites build. Millions of termites live in tunnels under and inside it.
terms.example: In parts of south India, termite mounds taller than a child stand in fields and forests.
terms.art: A tall reddish termite mound in a dry field, taller than the child standing next to it.

terms.meaning: A thick layer that slows down heat getting in or out.
terms.example: A thick blanket keeps you warm. A thick mud wall keeps a hut cool in summer.
terms.art: A mud hut with thick walls, sun arrows bouncing off and only small arrows getting in.

terms.meaning: The very slow change of living things over many, many generations. Living things that suit their home best leave the most young, so their features spread.
terms.example: Over millions of years, burrs with better hooks got carried further, so more burr plants have good hooks.
terms.art: A row of burrs from left to right, each with slightly better hooks, under a long arrow labelled 'millions of years'.

terms.meaning: The tiny building block that everything is made of. Atoms are far too small to see, even with an ordinary microscope.
terms.example: A leaf, a drop of water and your hand are all made of atoms.
terms.art: A zoom from a lotus leaf to a waxy bump, to a cluster of tiny balls.

terms.meaning: An official paper from the government. It says an invention belongs to its inventor for some years, so nobody else can copy it and sell it.
terms.example: George de Mestral got a patent for Velcro in 1955.
terms.art: An old official document with a stamp and a drawing of hooks and loops.

explanations.definition: Biomimicry is copying a trick from a plant or an animal to solve a human problem. The trick is copied, not the whole living thing.
explanations.description: Every living thing has problems to solve. It must hold on, stay clean, keep cool, move fast or stay dry. Over millions of years, plants and animals have found clever ways to do these things. Engineers look closely at these ways. They ask: what exactly is the trick? Then they copy that trick using materials people can make. An American scientist, Otto Schmitt, used the word 'biomimetics' for this in the 1950s. In 1997, Janine Benyus, an American writer about nature, wrote a book called 'Biomimicry'. It made the word famous around the world.
examples: A burr's hooks became Velcro.
A kingfisher's beak became the nose of a bullet train.
A lotus leaf's waxy bumps became paint that cleans itself in the rain.
explanations.art: Three panels: a burr becoming Velcro, a kingfisher becoming a train, a lotus leaf becoming a clean painted wall.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the whole unit: what biomimicry means.

explanations.concept: How a burr holds on, and how Velcro was invented
explanations.definition: A burr is covered in tiny stiff hooks. They catch in loops of fur or thread. Velcro copies this: one strip has hooks, the other has loops.
explanations.description: A burr is a seed case. It wants a ride to a new place, where its seeds can grow. So it is covered in hooks. When an animal brushes past, the hooks catch in its fur. Later the burr falls off far away. In 1941, George de Mestral, a Swiss engineer, looked at a burr under a microscope. He saw the hooks. He thought: two strips of cloth could join like this. Weavers in Lyon, a city in France, laughed at him. One weaver agreed to help. Cotton loops wore out too fast. Nylon, a strong plastic thread, worked much better. It took about ten years. He got a patent in 1955 and named his invention Velcro. The name joins two French words: 'velours', meaning velvet, and 'crochet', meaning hook.
examples: Velcro straps on school shoes, bags and blood pressure cuffs.
Astronauts used Velcro to stop things floating away inside their spacecraft.
A burr stuck to a woollen sock grips harder than one stuck to a smooth raincoat.
explanations.art: A burr under a microscope showing curled hooks, next to Velcro under a microscope showing hooks and loops.
explanations.context: Have you ever come home with prickly seeds stuck to your socks? This card shows how they hold on, and how they gave us Velcro.

explanations.concept: Why a lotus leaf stays clean
explanations.definition: A lotus leaf is covered in tiny bumps, and the bumps are coated in even tinier bits of wax. Water cannot spread on it, so it makes balls that roll off and carry dirt away. Scientists call this the lotus effect.
explanations.description: Lotus plants grow in muddy ponds. Yet their leaves always look clean. For a long time, nobody knew why. In the 1970s, a German plant scientist called Wilhelm Barthlott looked at leaves with a very powerful microscope. It is called a scanning electron microscope. He saw that the lotus leaf is not smooth at all. It is covered in tiny bumps, like a field of tiny hills, and the hills are frosted with wax. A water drop sits only on the tips of the bumps, with air underneath. So it stays round, like a ball, and rolls off at the smallest tilt. Dirt grips the water better than it grips the waxy tips. So the rolling drop picks the dirt up and carries it away. Barthlott and Christoph Neinhuis wrote about it in 1997. Soon after, a company made outside wall paint that copies the lotus. Rain washes it clean.
examples: Arbi (colocasia) leaves, nasturtium leaves and cabbage leaves show the same effect.
Self-cleaning paint, glass and cloth copy the lotus effect.
Touching a lotus leaf rubs off its wax. Then that spot gets wet like an ordinary leaf.
explanations.art: A zoom: a lotus leaf, then a close-up of bumps like tiny hills with frosty wax, then a round water drop sitting on the tips with air below.
explanations.context: Lotus leaves grow in muddy ponds, yet they always look clean. This card explains the surprising reason: they are bumpy, not smooth.

explanations.concept: Deep down: why water makes balls
explanations.definition: Water is made of tiny particles called molecules. Water molecules pull on each other strongly. On a waxy, bumpy surface, they pull on each other far more than on the surface. So the water pulls itself into a ball.
explanations.description: Zoom into a drop of water, far past anything a microscope can show. It is made of countless water molecules, each one built from three atoms. Every molecule tugs on the ones around it. At the edge of a drop, all that tugging pulls the water into a round shape, like a stretched skin. Scientists call this surface tension. On paper, the paper pulls the water too, so it spreads and soaks in. Wax hardly pulls on water at all. On the lotus, the drop also rests mostly on air between the bumps. Air does not pull the water either. So the water's own pull wins, and the drop becomes almost a perfect ball. The pull between molecules, and between wax and water, is an electric pull between their atoms. It is the same kind of force that gives us friction and holds a gecko on a wall.
examples: A drop on a candle stays round. A drop on a tissue spreads and soaks in.
Water striders, small insects, stand on a pond because surface tension holds them up.
explanations.art: A water drop cut open to show tiny balls (molecules) holding hands, sitting on wax bumps with air pockets underneath.
explanations.context: Why does water make a ball on a lotus leaf but soak into paper? This card zooms in to the tiny molecules of water to find out.

explanations.concept: The kingfisher and the bullet train
explanations.definition: A kingfisher dives from air into water with hardly a splash, because its beak is long and gets wider very slowly. Engineers copied that shape for the nose of a Japanese bullet train, so it came out of tunnels without a loud boom.
explanations.description: Japan's bullet trains are called Shinkansen. In the 1990s they were getting faster. But a problem got worse. When a train rushed into a tunnel, it shoved the air in front of it, like a plunger in a pipe. The squeezed air raced ahead and burst out of the far end with a boom. People living nearby complained. An engineer called Eiji Nakatsu was also a birdwatcher. He knew the kingfisher has the same problem. It goes from thin air into thick water at high speed. Yet it makes only a tiny splash. Its beak is long and narrow, and it gets wider very slowly towards its head. So the water is pushed aside a little at a time, not all at once. His team tested many nose shapes. The beak-like shape worked best. The 500 Series train, started in 1997, had a long beak-shaped nose. It was quieter, and it used less electricity. Nakatsu also copied an owl's soft-edged feathers to make the arm on the train's roof quieter.
examples: A kingfisher dives into a pond and leaves only a small ring on the water.
A pointed dough shape dropped into a bucket splashes far less than a flat one.
India's first bullet train line, between Mumbai and Ahmedabad, is being built using Japanese Shinkansen technology.
explanations.art: A kingfisher diving into water with a tiny splash, above a white bullet train with a long beak-shaped nose coming out of a tunnel quietly.
explanations.context: The common kingfisher lives by ponds and canals across India and Japan. This card shows how its beak helped make a bullet train quieter.

explanations.concept: The same shape, again and again
explanations.definition: Animals that are not close relatives often end up with the same shape, because they face the same problem. Scientists call this convergent evolution. Engineers who test shapes often reach the same answer too.
explanations.description: Sharks are fish. Dolphins are mammals, like us. Ichthyosaurs were reptiles that lived in the sea in the time of the dinosaurs. They are not close relatives at all. Yet all three have the same shape: a pointed nose, a smooth body and a strong tail. Why? Because the rules of water are the same for everyone. A fast swimmer with a blunt nose wastes its energy pushing water. Over millions of years, the fast, pointed ones caught more food and left more young. Engineers testing train noses in the 1990s did not wait millions of years. They tested shapes in days. But they arrived at the same answer as the kingfisher. Nature and engineers are solving the same problems, under the same rules.
examples: Penguins, seals and fish all have smooth, pointed bodies for swimming.
Bats, birds and insects all grew wings, in three different ways.
Racing cyclists and diving birds both tuck into a pointed shape.
explanations.art: A shark, a dolphin and an ichthyosaur swimming in a row, all the same shape, with a bullet train nose beside them.
explanations.context: A shark, a dolphin and a train nose look alike. This card explains why very different things end up with the same shape.

explanations.concept: How a gecko sticks to a wall
explanations.description: A gecko can run up glass and hang from the ceiling by one toe. Its feet have no glue and no suckers. Each toe has rows of tiny hairs called setae. Each hair splits into hundreds of even tinier tips. The tips are so small and bendy that they get extremely close to the wall, even into its tiny dips. When atoms get that close, they pull on each other very slightly. One tip's pull is tiny. But a gecko has millions of hairs and billions of tips. All those tiny pulls add up. Scientists agree on this much. They argue about one part: does water help?
examples: A house gecko walks upside down on the ceiling near the tube light.
Geckos find it hard to grip Teflon, the very slippery coating on non-stick pans.

perspectives.who: Kellar Autumn and his team, in the USA, in 2000 and 2002
perspectives.explanation: They measured the pull of a single gecko hair for the first time. Then they tested geckos on surfaces that water sticks to and surfaces water rolls off. Geckos gripped both about the same. So they said the grip comes from the pull between atoms, called van der Waals forces, not from water.

perspectives.who: Gerrit Huber and others, in Germany, in 2005
perspectives.explanation: They found single gecko hair tips grip harder when the air is damp. A very thin film of water from the air may help the tips hold on. So water helps too.
The pull between atoms does most of the work. A thin film of water can add to it on damp days. How much each matters is still being studied.

explanations.art: A zoom in four steps: a gecko on a window, a toe with lines of ridges, rows of tiny hairs, and one hair splitting into a brush of tips touching the glass.
explanations.context: A gecko can hang from a ceiling by one toe, with no glue. This card explains how its tiny hairs grip, and what scientists still argue about.

explanations.concept: How a gecko lets go, and the inventions it inspired
explanations.definition: A gecko lets go by peeling its toes up from the tip, like peeling sticky tape. Engineers have copied gecko hairs to make dry tape and robot grippers that need no glue.
explanations.description: Holding on is only half the trick. A gecko running up a wall must stick and unstick each foot many times every second. If you pull tape straight off a wall, it holds hard. If you peel it from one corner, it comes off easily. Gecko toes peel from the tip, a few hairs at a time. So letting go takes almost no effort. Gecko feet also stay clean. Dirt falls off the tiny tips as the gecko walks. In 2003, a team in Manchester, England, led by Andre Geim made a small patch of 'gecko tape' from plastic hairs. At Stanford University in the USA, engineers built a climbing robot called Stickybot in 2006. NASA engineers have built gecko-style grippers to grab things in space, where glue and suckers do not work well.
examples: Peel sticky tape from a corner and it comes away easily. Pull it straight and it holds.
Gecko-style grippers can pick up a smooth glass plate and let it go with no mark left behind.
explanations.art: A gecko toe curling up from the tip like peeling tape, next to a small robot with gecko-like pads climbing a glass wall.
explanations.context: Sticking is easy. Unsticking quickly is the hard part. This card shows how geckos let go, and what engineers have made from their feet.

explanations.description: Termites are small insects that live in huge families of millions. Some kinds build mounds taller than a grown-up. Deep inside, the termites grow a fungus garden. The garden needs air that stays fresh, damp and not too hot. Outside, the sun may be baking. Two things are agreed. First, the thick earth walls slow down the heat, so the inside changes temperature much less than the outside. Second, air moves through the tiny holes in the walls. But how the air is moved has changed in the books.
examples: In parts of south India, the termite Odontotermes obesus builds mounds taller than a child.
Inside a mound on a hot afternoon, it is far cooler than the ground in the sun.

perspectives.who: The old idea, from Martin Lüscher, a Swiss scientist, in 1961
perspectives.explanation: The termites' own warmth heats the air, which rises up a central chimney and draws fresh air in, like a fire drawing air up a chimney.

perspectives.who: Hunter King, Samuel Ocko and L. Mahadevan, scientists at Harvard University, in 2015
perspectives.explanation: They put tiny sensors into real mounds near Bengaluru. They found the mound breathes with the day and night. In the day, the thin outer walls warm faster than the middle, and air moves one way. At night, the walls cool faster, and air moves the other way.

perspectives.who: J. Scott Turner, an American scientist who studied African mounds
perspectives.explanation: Wind gusting over the mound also pushes and pulls the air inside. Different kinds of mound may work in different ways. The full story is still being worked out.

explanations.art: A cut-away termite mound with red arrows of air moving one way in the daytime sun, and blue arrows moving the other way under a night sky.
explanations.context: A termite mound stays cool inside on a burning hot day, with no fans. This card shows how, and how scientists changed their minds about it.

explanations.definition: Some architects design buildings with thick walls, and air channels that let cool night air flush through. These ideas were inspired by termite mounds. They keep buildings cooler with less air conditioning.
explanations.description: In 1996, the Eastgate Centre opened in Harare, the capital city of Zimbabwe in Africa. Its architect, Mick Pearce, studied termite mounds. The building has thick concrete walls and floors that soak up heat slowly in the day. At night, fans pull cool outside air through hollow spaces in the floors, and warm air leaves through chimneys on the roof. Its designers reported that it uses much less energy for cooling than similar buildings. Here is a surprise. The building was based on the old chimney idea of how mounds work. Scientists later found mounds work differently. The building still works well. A copy of a half-understood idea can still be a good idea. In India, old houses with thick mud walls, small windows and courtyards also stay cool in the heat.
examples: Thick mud walls of village houses keep rooms cool in summer.
A matka, an earthen pot, keeps water cool because water seeps through and dries off its outside.
explanations.art: A tall building with chimneys on its roof next to a termite mound with the same shape, cool blue arrows flowing through both at night.
explanations.context: Termites keep their homes cool without electricity. This card is about a building in Africa that copied them.

explanations.concept: Copy the trick, not the look
explanations.definition: Good biomimicry copies how something works, not just how it looks. A machine that only looks like an animal usually does not work like one.
explanations.description: Around the year 1500, Leonardo da Vinci, the Italian artist and inventor, drew flying machines with flapping wings like a bird's. None of them flew. Copying the look of flapping was not enough. Four hundred years later, people studied the tricks instead. Otto Lilienthal, a German engineer, studied storks and wrote a book about bird flight in 1889. He made gliders that really flew. Wilbur and Orville Wright, two brothers in the USA, watched birds twist the tips of their wings to balance. They copied that twist, not the flapping. In 1903 they made the first powered aeroplane flight. Here in India, the Lotus Temple in Delhi copies the look of a lotus flower. It is beautiful, but its walls do not clean themselves. Self-cleaning paint looks nothing like a lotus, but it copies the lotus leaf's trick.
examples: The bullet train's nose does not have feathers or eyes. It copies only the beak's slow widening.
Velcro does not look like a burr. It copies only the hooks.
explanations.art: Two panels: Leonardo's flapping machine with a red cross, and the Wright brothers' plane with twisted wingtips and a tick.
explanations.context: This card is about the biggest lesson for inventors who copy nature: copy how it works, not how it looks.

explanations.definition: Nature's designs come from evolution. Over many generations, living things with features that work better leave more young. So those features spread.
explanations.description: Nobody designed the burr's hooks. Long ago, some burr plants had slightly better hooks than others, just by chance. Their burrs got carried further by animals, so more of their seeds grew. Their young had good hooks too, because living things pass their features on to their young. Over millions of years, the hooks got better and better. Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace explained this in 1858. Scientists call it evolution by natural selection. Life on Earth began about 3.8 billion years ago. Every plant and animal alive today comes from a long line of living things that survived. Janine Benyus likes to say nature has been testing its designs for 3.8 billion years. Engineers are just learning to read the results.
examples: Kingfishers whose beaks made less splash caught more fish, and raised more chicks.
Geckos that gripped better escaped from snakes, and lived to lay eggs.
explanations.art: A long timeline from tiny cells 3.8 billion years ago to a burr, a kingfisher and a gecko today, with a child at the end holding a notebook.
explanations.context: Who designed the burr's hooks and the gecko's toes? This card explains where nature's designs come from.

explanations.description: People who love biomimicry often say nature's designs are the best. Others say that is not quite right. Both sides have good points.
examples: Your eye has a blind spot, where the nerve leaves it. An octopus eye is built the other way round and has no blind spot.
Bacteria have a tiny spinning motor to swim, but no animal grew a wheel to roll on.

perspectives.who: Janine Benyus and many people who work in biomimicry
perspectives.explanation: Nature has tested its designs for billions of years. Nature's designs are also made from water, sunlight and simple stuff, at ordinary temperatures, and they rot away safely when they are finished. We should learn from that.
Evolution makes things good enough to survive, not perfect. It can only change what is already there, a little at a time. So living things carry old mistakes, like the blind spot in your eye.
People have made things nature never made: wheels that roll, metal tools, fire for cooking, rockets. The best ideas often mix nature's tricks with human ones.

explanations.art: A balance scale with a kingfisher and a gecko on one side, and a wheel, a rocket and a flame on the other.
explanations.context: Many people say nature is the greatest designer. This card asks whether that is true, and gives three different views.

explanations.description: An inventor who copies a burr can get a patent. A patent is an official paper that says nobody else may copy and sell the invention for some years. But nobody pays the burr. And sometimes the 'new' idea was known by people for hundreds of years. In 1995, two scientists in the USA got a patent for using turmeric to heal wounds. Indian grandmothers had done that for centuries. India's science council, the CSIR, showed the judges very old Indian books that described it. In 1997, the patent was cancelled.
examples: Haldi on a cut is an old Indian home remedy.
Jagadish Chandra Bose, the Indian scientist, refused to patent his radio inventions. He believed knowledge should be free.

perspectives.explanation: Patents reward people for years of hard work. George de Mestral spent about ten years making Velcro work. Without patents, fewer people would try.

perspectives.who: Many people in India and other countries
perspectives.explanation: Knowledge that communities have had for centuries should not be taken and owned by one company. In 2001, India started a huge library of traditional knowledge, so it cannot be patented by others.
Ideas copied from nature, and ideas that help people, should be free for everyone.

explanations.art: A burr, a lotus and a turmeric root sitting in a courtroom's witness box, while people argue over a paper with a big stamp.
explanations.context: When someone copies a plant's idea, who should own it? This card is about patents, turmeric and fairness.

explanations.description: Biomimicry is still young. Scientists are trying many new ideas, and most are not yet in our homes. The pitcher plant traps insects with a rim so slippery that they slide in. India's own pitcher plant grows in the hills of Meghalaya. In 2011, a team led by Joanna Aizenberg at Harvard University made a coating that copies it. Almost nothing sticks to it, not even oil. In the Namib Desert in Africa, a beetle drinks fog. Water from the fog gathers on bumps on its back. Scientists described it in 2001, and others are testing fog-catching surfaces like it. Some scientists are trying to build an 'artificial leaf' that makes fuel from sunlight and water, like a plant makes food. Nobody yet knows which of these will work well enough to use every day.
examples: A ketchup or honey bottle that empties completely, with nothing stuck to the sides.
Nets that catch drinking water from fog on dry hills.
explanations.art: A pitcher plant with an ant sliding into it, a desert beetle with a fog drop on its back, and a green artificial leaf making bubbles in sunlight.
explanations.context: Velcro and lotus paint are old now. This card is about new copies of nature that scientists are still testing.

agreed.text: Many useful inventions copy tricks from plants and animals.
agreed.evidence: George de Mestral wrote about the burr in his Velcro patent of 1955. Eiji Nakatsu described how the kingfisher shaped the 500 Series train nose.

agreed.text: Lotus leaves stay clean because they are covered in tiny waxy bumps.
agreed.evidence: Powerful microscopes show the bumps and the wax. You can see drops roll off and carry dust away. If you rub the wax off, that spot gets wet.

agreed.text: Geckos stick to walls without glue or suckers, using millions of tiny hairs.
agreed.evidence: Gecko feet leave no glue behind. Scientists have measured the pull of a single hair. Geckos grip badly on Teflon, a coating that atoms hardly pull on.

agreed.text: A pointed, streamlined shape moves through air and water with less drag than a blunt one.
agreed.evidence: Engineers measure this with models in water tanks and wind tunnels. You can see it at home: a pointed dough shape splashes far less than a flat one.

agreed.text: Nature's designs come from evolution over very long times.
agreed.evidence: Fossils, the stony remains of ancient life, show living things slowly changing. DNA, the instructions inside every cell, shows how living things are related.

challenging.claim: NASA, the American space agency, invented Velcro.
challenging.who: A popular story, often heard in schools
challenging.for: Astronauts used Velcro in the 1960s, in the Apollo spacecraft that went to the Moon. It held their pens and food packets in place, so they did not float away.
challenging.against: George de Mestral invented Velcro, and got his patent in 1955. That was years before NASA started using it. NASA made Velcro famous, but did not invent it.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous story of who invented Velcro.

challenging.claim: The smoother and shinier a surface, the cleaner it stays.
challenging.who: A common belief. Most of us think this without noticing.
challenging.for: Smooth glass and polished steel are easy to wipe clean.
challenging.against: The lotus leaf stays clean because it is bumpy, not smooth. On a smooth surface, water drops stick and leave dirty marks when they dry. On the bumpy, waxy lotus, drops roll off and take the dirt with them.
challenging.context: This card is about what makes a surface stay clean.

challenging.claim: To copy nature, make your machine look like the animal.
challenging.who: Many early inventors, including some who tried to fly
challenging.for: Birds fly by flapping, so a flying machine should flap too.
challenging.against: Flapping machines did not fly. The Wright brothers copied a trick instead: birds twist their wingtips to balance. Good biomimicry copies how a thing works, not what it looks like.
challenging.context: This card is about a mistake many inventors made when they copied birds.

challenging.claim: The Eastgate Centre in Zimbabwe cools itself exactly the way a termite mound does.
challenging.who: Many books and websites about biomimicry
challenging.for: Its architect, Mick Pearce, studied termite mounds. The building has thick walls, air channels and chimneys, and uses little energy for cooling.
challenging.against: It was based on the old chimney idea of how mounds work. Scientists later found real mounds breathe with day and night, and with the wind. The building also uses fans. It was inspired by termites, but it does not work quite like a mound.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous building in Africa that is said to copy termite mounds.

challenging.claim: A gecko sticks with sticky glue or tiny suction cups.
challenging.who: A common guess, and an idea some scientists once had
challenging.for: Some animals, like octopuses, really do use suckers. And sticky things usually have glue.
challenging.against: Gecko feet leave no glue. Experiments showed geckos still cling when the air is pumped away, so it is not suction. The grip comes from billions of tiny hair tips getting extremely close to the wall.
challenging.context: This card is about old guesses for how geckos cling to walls and ceilings.

challenging.claim: A car shaped like a boxfish proved that fish shapes are the best for cars.
challenging.who: The company Mercedes-Benz, with its boxfish concept car in 2005
challenging.for: The boxfish is a small reef fish that looks like a box. The car copied its shape, and in tests it slipped through the air very easily.
challenging.against: Later, scientists studied real boxfish. They found the boxfish's shape helps it turn quickly, more than it helps it swim straight with little drag. The car never went on sale. Copying a living thing needs a careful look at what its shape is really for.
challenging.context: This card is about a car that copied a fish, and what scientists later found out about the fish.

big_questions.q: A burr's hooks gave us Velcro. Should the burr get any credit? Who should own an idea that came from nature?
big_questions.hint: Think about George de Mestral's ten years of work. Then think about the plant's millions of years.

big_questions.q: Is a bullet train natural or man-made? Where exactly would you draw the line?
big_questions.hint: The train is made by people. People are made by nature. The nose was copied from a bird.

big_questions.q: Why does a lotus leaf stay clean, when a shiny steel plate does not?
big_questions.hint: Look at a lotus or arbi leaf with a magnifying glass. Is it really smooth?

big_questions.q: Sharks, dolphins and kingfishers are not close relatives. Why do they share the same pointed shape?
big_questions.hint: What problem do they all have to solve?

big_questions.q: How can something as tiny as the pull between atoms hold up a whole gecko?
big_questions.hint: Think about one strand of thread, and then a thick rope made of millions of strands.

big_questions.q: If nature has been testing designs for 3.8 billion years, does that make nature wise?
big_questions.hint: Is cleverness only the kind that happens in a head? What kind of cleverness does a river have when it finds the easiest way downhill?

big_questions.q: Plants and animals are dying out faster than ever because of people. What designs might we lose before we even see them?
big_questions.hint: Scientists have named less than a quarter of the kinds of living things on Earth, by many estimates.

big_questions.q: Is it fair to copy a living thing's trick and not give anything back to it?
big_questions.hint: What could people do for lotus ponds, geckos and termites, in return?

big_questions.q: The Bhagavad Gita says a wise person is like a lotus leaf in water. What could that mean?
big_questions.hint: The leaf lives in the muddy pond, yet the mud does not stick to it.

big_questions.q: Nature never grew a wheel to roll on. But people did. Are there things only people can invent?
big_questions.hint: Bacteria have a tiny spinning motor. Is that a kind of wheel?

big_questions.q: Termite mounds have no fans and no electricity, and stay cool. What could our homes learn from them?
big_questions.hint: Think about thick walls, shade, and when the air outside is coolest.

story.title: The Quietest Splash
story.note: Eiji Nakatsu, the tunnel boom, his birdwatching, the kingfisher idea, the owl feathers and the 500 Series train of 1997 are real. The kingfisher who tells the story, Mei, her baby brother and her letters are made up.
text: I am a kingfisher. I am the size of a sparrow. My back is the blue of a gas flame, and my front is the orange of a ripe mango. My kind lives by slow rivers and ponds in many countries. We live in England, all across India, and in Japan, where I live. This is the story of my river, of the hole in the mountain beside it, and of a man who sat very still.

My river runs past rice fields and a bamboo grove, and then under a mountain. The people dug a long hole through the mountain. They call it a tunnel. Through it run the white trains, some of the fastest trains in the world. People call them bullet trains.

I did not mind the trains going in. They went in with a rush and a hiss. What I minded was the other end. A moment after a train went in, the far side of the mountain coughed. BOOM. It was a sound like a giant slamming a door. The herons in the rice fields jumped into the air. The windows of the houses rattled. And in the house by the bamboo, a baby began to cry. He cried every time a train went through, from morning until night.

The baby's sister was called Mei. She was nine. She often sat on the riverbank with a notebook, drawing me. She was not very good at sitting still, so I usually flew off before she finished. But I liked her. She wrote letters too. I saw her post them in the red box by the road. Later I heard her mother say that Mei had written to the train company. 'Please make your train quieter,' she had written. 'My brother cannot sleep.'

I knew why the mountain boomed. Birds understand air. When a train rushed into the tunnel, it pushed the air in front of it, like a hand pushing water along a narrow drain. The air had nowhere to go. It squeezed tighter and tighter, and it raced ahead of the train. At the far end, it burst out into the open. BOOM. The faster the trains went, the louder the boom became. And every year the trains went faster.

One spring a man began to come to my river. He came on his days off. He had binoculars, a notebook and a flask of tea. He sat on a rock under the willow for hours and hours, and he did not move. Most people walk along a river talking and pointing, and every bird flies away. This man watched. People who watch birds properly learn to be part of the riverbank.
So I fished as usual. I sat on my branch above the water, as still as he was. I saw a silver flick below. I dropped.

This is how I fish. I fall from the thin, soft air into the thick, heavy water, as fast as I can. Water is hard to push. If I hit it flat, it would slap me like a wall, and the fish would see the splash and dart away. But my beak is long and straight and sharp. From its tip, it gets wider very slowly, and then my head gets wider slowly, and then my body. So I do not push the water all at once. I push it aside a little at a time, from the tip backwards. I went in with a tiny sound, ploop. I left a ring on the water no bigger than a coin. I came out with a fish.

The man stood up on his rock. He nearly dropped his tea. He began to write in his notebook very fast. I heard him say something to himself. 'From thin air into thick water,' he said. 'From open air into a tight tunnel. It is the same problem.'

I did not understand his words then. I only noticed he was happy. That night, an owl hunted over the rice fields. Owls fly with no sound at all, because the edges of their feathers are soft and fringed. The man was there in the dark too, listening to nothing.
Then he stopped coming for a long time. The trains still boomed. Mei's brother still cried. Mei stopped writing letters and started drawing trains instead. Her trains had long, pointed faces.
Three summers went by. I raised two families of chicks in my burrow in the riverbank. I taught them to sit still, to watch, and to drop.

Then one morning a new train came. It was grey and blue, and it had the longest nose I had ever seen. The nose did not end in a round face like the old trains. It stretched out long and thin, and it widened very slowly, all the way back to the windows. It looked like my beak. It slid into the tunnel with a long, soft hiss.
I waited on my branch for the far side of the mountain to cough. The herons waited. The house by the bamboo waited.
Nothing came. Only a hush, like wind in the bamboo.

The door of the house opened, and Mei came out with her baby brother in her arms. He was fast asleep. She stood looking at the mountain for a long time. Then she looked at the river, at my branch, at me.

Later that day she sat on the bank and drew in her notebook again. She drew the new train. Next to it, she drew me, diving. She was careful to make the beak and the nose exactly the same shape. For once, I sat still until she had finished.

People tell this story now in many countries. They say that a train copied a kingfisher. I am not sure it is quite like that. The water taught my family its lesson over millions of years. The air taught the man the same lesson in a few. We were both listening to the same teacher. I just heard it first.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the train's boom and the kingfisher's splash are the same problem. A fast thing moves from thin stuff into thick stuff: air into water, or open air into a tight tunnel. Hitting it with a blunt front shoves it all at once, which makes a slap or a boom. A long, slowly widening front pushes it aside a little at a time. The engineer did not copy the bird's look. He copied the trick. The story also quietly asks who teaches whom, and whether 'natural' and 'man-made' are really separate.
ask: Why did the tunnel boom when the old trains came out?
How does the kingfisher dive without a big splash? What is special about the shape of its beak?
The man said, 'It is the same problem.' What did he mean?
Why do you think the man sat so still for so long?
At the end, the kingfisher says they were both listening to the same teacher. Who or what was the teacher?

games.title: Nature's Idea Match
games.context: This is a matching card game about biomimicry, copying a trick from nature to solve a human problem. Each nature card has an invention card that copied its trick. You find the pairs and say the trick.

printables.title: 10 green NATURE cards to cut out
items: Burr: a seed case covered in tiny hooks
Lotus leaf: tiny bumps coated in wax
Kingfisher: a long beak that widens slowly
Owl: feathers with soft, fringed edges
Gecko: toes with millions of tiny hairs
Termite mound: thick earth walls and air passages
Pitcher plant: a rim so slippery that insects slide in
Honeybee comb: rows of six-sided cells
Humpback whale: bumps along the front edge of its flippers
Bird: twists the tips of its wings to balance

printables.title: 10 orange INVENTION cards to cut out
items: Velcro straps on shoes and bags
Wall paint that rain washes clean
The long nose of a quiet bullet train
A quieter arm on top of a bullet train, where it touches the electric wire
Tape and robot grippers that hold on with no glue
A building in Zimbabwe that stays cool with little air conditioning
A super-slippery coating that nothing sticks to
Light, strong panels inside aeroplane floors and doors
Bumpy-edged blades for wind turbines and fans
The Wright brothers' first aeroplane, which twisted its wingtips

printables.title: Trick sheet

The trick, said in my own words
Points

rules: Cut out the 10 green nature cards and the 10 orange invention cards.
Shuffle each colour. Lay all 20 cards face down in rows, green on one side and orange on the other.
On your turn, turn over one green card and one orange card. Read both out loud.
If they are a pair, say the trick that was copied, in your own words. Keep the pair and win 2 points. Then have another turn.
If they are not a pair, turn them back face down. Try to remember where they were.
A pair with no trick said wins only 1 point.
When all the pairs are found, the player with the most points wins. Playing alone? Count your turns. Next time, try to finish in fewer turns.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 20 cards. 2. Shuffle the green cards and lay them face down in two rows of 5. 3. Do the same with the orange cards, next to them.
flow.say: Every green card is a living thing with a clever trick. Every orange card is an invention that copied one of those tricks. We will hunt for the pairs.
flow.kid: Lay the green cards face down. Lay the orange cards face down beside them. Each green card has one orange partner. Can you find them all?
flow.context: This is the first step of Nature's Idea Match, a memory game about inventions copied from plants and animals. Here you set up the cards.

flow.do: Play one practice pair face up. Show the burr card and the Velcro card side by side.
flow.say: Here is a pair to practise with. A burr and Velcro. What trick did Velcro copy?
flow.kid: Practice pair: burr and Velcro. What trick did Velcro copy? Tap your answer.

ask.q: What did Velcro copy from the burr?
good: Its tiny hooks.
Hooks that catch in loops, like a burr catching in fur.

check.q: What trick did Velcro copy from the burr?
options: Its tiny hooks, which catch in loops
Its green colour
Its sticky glue
check.why: A burr has no glue. It is covered in tiny stiff hooks that catch in fur and thread. Velcro copies that: one strip has hooks and the other has soft loops. Picking 'sticky glue' is a common guess, because things that stick usually have glue.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. Turn one green card and one orange card. 2. If they match, the player says the trick and keeps the pair. 3. If not, turn them back. 4. Write each found pair on the trick sheet.
flow.say: When you find a pair, don't just say the names. Tell us the trick: how does the living thing do it, and what did the invention copy?
flow.kid: Turn one green card and one orange card. A pair? Say the trick to win 2 points. If not, turn them back and remember them.
flow.parent: The pairs are: burr and Velcro (hooks). Lotus and self-cleaning paint (waxy bumps). Kingfisher and train nose (a front that widens slowly). Owl and the quiet train arm (soft, fringed edges). Gecko and gripper tape (tiny hairs). Termite mound and the Zimbabwe building (thick walls and air channels). Pitcher plant and slippery coating. Honeycomb and aeroplane panels (six-sided cells). Whale flipper and turbine blades (bumpy edges). Bird wings and the Wright brothers' plane (twisted wingtips). Accept any trick said in the child's own words.

flow.do: When a player finds the honeycomb pair, stop and look at the six-sided cells together.
flow.say: Bees build with six-sided cells. Why six sides? Hexagons fit together with no gaps, and use very little wax for a lot of space.
flow.kid: Look at the honeycomb card. Each cell has six sides. They fit together with no gaps. Engineers copy this to make strong, light panels.
flow.think: Bees never learned geometry. So how did they end up with the best shape?

flow.do: Count the points to find the winner. Then ask each player which trick they would most like to use in their own invention.
flow.say: Which trick would you most like to borrow for an invention of your own? What would you make with it?
flow.kid: Count your points. Playing alone? Write how many turns it took. Which trick would you borrow for your own invention?
flow.think: All these tricks were found by people who looked very closely at living things. What living thing near you might be hiding a trick nobody has noticed yet?

2 Lotus leaf: waxy bumps that make water roll off

Living thing
My invention (draw it)

rules: You need one die, or two dice, the two printed lists and the score sheet.
Roll the die once. Find that number on the Problem list.
Roll again. Find that number on the Nature list.
In 2 minutes, draw an invention that uses that living thing's trick to solve that problem.
Explain it. Score 1 point for naming the trick, 1 point for saying how you would test it, and 1 point if it could really be built.

flow.do: 1. Put the two printed lists and the score sheet on the table. 2. Have a die, a pencil and a timer ready.
flow.say: Inventors often start with a problem, then look at nature for a trick. Today the dice will choose the problem and the living thing. You do the inventing.
flow.kid: Put out the two lists and your score sheet. Get a die and a pencil. The dice choose a problem and a living thing. You invent!
flow.context: This is the first step of Design Dice, an inventing game. You join a home problem with a trick from nature.

flow.do: Play one round together as practice. Use problem 1, the warm water bottle, and nature 5, the termite mound.
flow.say: Practice round. The water bottle gets warm in the sun. The termite mound has thick walls that slow heat. What could we invent?
flow.kid: Practice: a warm water bottle, and a termite mound. How could thick walls help a water bottle? Draw your idea.

ask.q: How could you test if your bottle cover works?
good: Put two bottles in the sun, one with the cover. Feel which is cooler after an hour.
Put an ice cube in each and see which melts last.

check.q: A water bottle gets warm in the sun. Which idea copies the termite mound's trick?
options: Wrap it in a thick jacket of cloth, so heat gets in slowly
Paint it shiny gold
Make it pointed like a beak
check.why: A termite mound's thick earth walls slow down the heat getting in. A thick cloth jacket does the same for a bottle. Wetting the cloth helps even more, like a matka. Picking 'pointed like a beak' mixes up the tricks. A pointed shape helps with moving through air or water, not with heat.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to roll both dice. 2. Each player draws an invention in 2 minutes. 3. They explain it. 4. The others score it with the three points on the sheet.
flow.say: Roll, draw for two minutes, then tell us about it. Remember the three points: name the trick, say how to test it, and could it really be built?
flow.kid: Roll both dice. Draw your invention in 2 minutes. Then explain it, with the trick and how to test it.
flow.parent: Some strong answers. A burr-hook strip on the bag strap and a loop strip on the chair, for problem 2. A label rubbed thickly with candle wax, for problem 3. A pointed nose for the toy car, for problem 5. Grooved soft rubber pads on the chappal, like a tree frog's toe pads, for problem 6. Silly but well-explained ideas deserve the trick point too.

flow.do: Add up the points. Then choose the one invention everyone would most like to really build.
flow.say: Which invention should we really build and test? We can try it in the My Nature Invention project.
flow.kid: Add up your points. Which of your inventions would you most like to really build? Circle it.
flow.think: Some pairs seemed impossible at first, then turned into good ideas. Why does joining two very different things help us invent?

items.p: What is biomimicry?
opts: Copying a trick from a plant or animal to solve a human problem
Making a machine look like an animal
items.why: Biomimicry means copying how a living thing solves a problem. 'Bio' means life and 'mimic' means copy. Picking 'making a machine look like an animal' is a common mix-up. Good biomimicry copies the trick, not the look.
items.art: A burr and a Velcro strap with an arrow between them.

items.p: Which plant part gave George de Mestral the idea for Velcro?
opts: A burr, a seed case with tiny hooks
items.why: In 1941, burrs stuck to his trousers and his dog. Under a microscope, he saw tiny hooks. Picking 'sticky leaf' means thinking the burr sticks with glue. It sticks with hooks.

items.p: Velcro has tiny ____ on one strip and soft loops on the other.
items.why: The hooks on one side catch in the loops on the other side, just as a burr's hooks catch in fur.

items.p: Why does a lotus leaf stay clean in a muddy pond?
opts: Tiny waxy bumps make water roll off in balls, carrying dirt away
It is very smooth and shiny, like glass
It grows a new leaf every day
items.why: The lotus leaf is covered in tiny bumps with wax on them. Water drops sit on the tips, stay round and roll off, taking dirt with them. Picking 'smooth like glass' is the most common idea. The surprise is that the leaf is bumpy, not smooth.

items.p: A lotus leaf is perfectly smooth when you look at it under a powerful microscope.
items.why: False. Under a powerful microscope, it is covered in tiny bumps, like a field of tiny hills, frosted with wax.

items.p: Remember the leaf experiment, where you dripped water on four surfaces and tilted them. On the arbi leaf, the drops looked like…
opts: Round silver balls that rolled away
items.why: On an arbi or lotus leaf, the drops stay round like little silver balls. They roll off at a small tilt. Picking 'flat puddles' describes what happens on paper or an ordinary leaf.
items.context: In the leaf experiment, you put drops of water on an arbi leaf, an ordinary leaf, a steel plate and paper.

items.p: Match each living thing to the invention that copied it.
items.why: Each invention copied one trick: hooks, waxy bumps, a slowly widening front, tiny bendy hairs, and thick walls with air channels.

items.p: Why did the old bullet trains make a loud boom when they came out of tunnels?
opts: They squeezed the air in front of them, and it burst out of the far end
items.why: A fast train pushes the air ahead of it, like a plunger in a pipe. The squeezed air rushes ahead and bursts out of the tunnel with a boom. Picking 'engines exploded' is a guess. Nothing broke. It was the air.

items.p: Remember the splash experiment. Which dough shape made the smallest splash?
items.why: The beak went in tip first and widened slowly, so it pushed the water aside gently. The pancake hit lots of water at once and splashed most. Picking the ball is close, but it still meets more water at once than the beak.
items.context: In the splash experiment, you dropped three dough shapes with the same amount of dough into a bucket and counted the splash spots.

items.p: A gecko's toes are covered in millions of tiny ____.
items.why: The tiny hairs are called setae. Each one splits into hundreds of tinier tips that get very close to the wall.

items.p: A gecko sticks to walls using glue on its feet.
items.why: False. Gecko feet leave no glue. They grip because billions of tiny hair tips get so close to the wall that their atoms pull on the wall's atoms.

items.p: Sort these. Which trick do they use?
items: Burr
Hooks that catch
Velcro
Hooks that catch
Lotus leaf
Water that rolls off
Candle-waxed paper
Water that rolls off
Termite mound
Thick walls that slow heat
Mud house
Thick walls that slow heat
items.why: Burrs and Velcro use hooks. Lotus leaves and waxed paper make water roll off. Termite mounds and mud houses have thick walls that slow the heat down.

items.p: Remember the ice experiment with cup houses in the sun. Which cup kept its ice longest?
opts: A cup with thick walls, like newspaper or wet cloth
The bare cup with thin walls
They all melted at exactly the same time
items.why: Thick walls slow down the heat getting in, so the ice melts more slowly. A wet cloth also cools as its water dries, like a matka. Picking 'all the same' forgets that only the walls were different.
items.context: In the ice experiment, you put an ice cube in each of three cups with different walls, and left them in the sun.

items.p: Name one thing in your home with Velcro on it. Say what the Velcro does there.
items.a: My school shoes have Velcro. It holds the strap closed, so the shoe stays on my foot.
items.why: Velcro is used on shoes, bags, watches, blood pressure cuffs and jackets, wherever something must open and close easily.

items.p: Finish like a scientist. Think about one experiment you did in this unit. Write what you think, what you saw, and why.
items.a: What I think: a pointed shape splashes least. What I saw: the beak made 2 splash spots and the pancake made 22. Why: the beak pushes water aside a little at a time, like a kingfisher's beak.
items.why: A good answer has all three parts: a claim, the evidence you saw, and the reasoning that links them.

items.p: Draw a burr's hook catching a loop of wool. Label the hook and the loop.
items.a: A curved hook, like the letter J, hooked through a round loop of wool, both labelled.
items.why: The hook catches in the loop, so they hold together. Pulling sideways makes them hold. Peeling them apart unhooks them one at a time.
items.art: A blank box with a small loop of wool drawn in the corner.

items.p: On a lotus leaf, what is underneath a water drop, between the tiny bumps?
opts: Nothing at all, not even air
items.why: The drop sits on the bump tips with pockets of air underneath. Air doesn't pull on water, so the drop stays round and rolls. Picking 'nothing at all' misses that air fills the gaps. You saw it as a silver shine on the sooty spoon under water.

items.p: Remember the sooty spoon. Under water, the sooty side looked shiny silver. Why?
opts: A thin layer of air was trapped in the tiny bumps of soot
The spoon was made of silver
items.why: Water cannot push into the tiny spaces between the soot bumps, so a thin skin of air stays there. Light bounces off it, so it looks like a mirror. Picking 'the spoon was silver' is a guess. Steel looks different under water when it has no soot.
items.context: In the Lotus Spoon activity, a grown-up coated the back of a steel spoon with candle soot. Then you dipped it in water.

items.p: Why does touching a lotus leaf with your fingers spoil the lotus trick in that spot?
items.why: The leaf's trick needs both the bumps and the wax. Rubbing wipes away the wax, so water can grip that spot and spread. Picking 'fingers are wet' is a fair thought, but even dry fingers rub off wax.

items.p: In the splash experiment, every shape had the same amount of dough and was dropped from 30 cm. Why?
opts: To make it a fair test, so only the shape changed
items.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If the dough amounts or heights were different, you couldn't tell whether the shape caused the difference. Picking 'to make the splash bigger' misses the reason: fairness.
items.context: In the splash experiment, you dropped a flat pancake, a ball and a pointed beak of dough into a bucket of water.

items.p: Look at the made-up results from the splash experiment. How many more splash spots did the pancake make than the beak?
items.why: The pancake made 22 spots and the beak made 2. 22 take away 2 is 20. Picking 22 forgets to take away the beak's 2 spots.
items.context: In the splash experiment, you counted the wet spots that splashes left on newspaper around the bucket.

chart.title: Made-up results: splash spots on the newspaper

items.p: Eiji Nakatsu said the kingfisher and the train have the same problem. What is it?
opts: Moving fast from thin stuff into thick stuff: air into water, or open air into a tunnel
items.why: The kingfisher dives from air into water. The train rushes from open air into a tight tunnel. Both must push through something thicker without a slap or a boom. Picking 'catching fish' is the bird's goal, but not the problem the train shares.

items.p: Sharks, dolphins and kingfishers are not close relatives. Why do they all have a pointed, smooth shape?
opts: They all have to move fast through water, so the same shape works best for all of them
They all have the same parents
items.why: The rules of water are the same for every animal. Over millions of years, the ones with a shape that moves easily through water caught more food and had more young. Scientists call this convergent evolution. Animals cannot copy each other's bodies, and they are not close relatives.

items.p: Put the inventor's steps in order: test it fairly, find a problem, improve it and test again, find a living thing with a trick, build a prototype, draw a design.
items: find a problem
find a living thing with a trick
draw a design
build a prototype
test it fairly
improve it and test again
items.why: Inventors start with a problem, look for a trick that solves it, plan, build a rough version, test it, then improve it. The last two steps can go round and round many times.

items.p: Remember the gecko toe prints. Why did the brush print reach into the dips but the flat eraser didn't?
opts: The bristles bend into the dips, but a flat pad only touches the tops
items.why: A flat, stiff pad touches only the tops of bumps. Bendy bristles splay into the dips. Gecko hairs do the same on a bumpy wall, so much more of the foot touches it. Picking 'more paint' is a sensible worry, which is why you should load both with paint.
items.context: In the Gecko Toe Prints activity, you printed with a flat eraser and with a soft brush on wavy cardboard.

items.p: How does a gecko let go of the wall so quickly?
opts: It peels its toes up from the tips, like peeling tape from a corner
It pulls its whole foot straight off at once
It waits for the glue to dry
items.why: Peeling from the tip unhooks only a few hairs at a time, so it takes almost no effort. Pulling straight off would mean breaking all the grips at once. Geckos have no glue.

items.p: Termite mounds are cooled by fans that the termites build.
items.why: False. There are no fans. Thick earth walls slow the heat. Air moves through tiny holes because the walls warm and cool with day and night, and because of the wind.

items.p: A first, rough model of an invention, made to test an idea, is called a ____.
items.why: A prototype is a quick first try. Engineers expect it to have problems, because testing it shows how to make it better.

items.p: Leonardo da Vinci drew flying machines with flapping wings. None of them flew. The Wright brothers' plane flew. What did the Wright brothers copy from birds?
opts: How birds twist their wingtips to balance
items.why: They copied a trick, the twist of the wingtips, not the look of flapping. Picking 'flapping' is what many early inventors tried, and it did not work for people-sized machines.

items.p: The Lotus Temple in Delhi is shaped like a lotus flower. Self-cleaning paint looks nothing like a lotus. Which one is biomimicry? Explain.
items.a: The self-cleaning paint is biomimicry. It copies the lotus leaf's trick of tiny waxy bumps, so rain washes it clean. The temple only copies the look of the flower.
items.why: Biomimicry copies how something works. Copying only the look is art or decoration, which is lovely too, but different.

items.p: Your water bottle gets warm in the sun on the way to school. Use a trick from nature to design a cover for it. Say how you would test it.
items.a: I would copy the termite mound's thick walls, and the matka. I would make a thick cotton cover and wet it before I leave. To test it, I would put two bottles in the sun, one with the cover, and feel which is cooler after an hour.
items.why: A good answer names a trick from nature, explains how the design uses it, and describes a fair test with only one thing changed.

items.p: Deep down, why does water pull itself into a ball on a waxy leaf?
opts: Water molecules pull on each other more strongly than the wax pulls on them
Wax pushes water away with magnets
items.why: Water molecules tug on each other. Wax hardly pulls on water at all. So the water's own pull wins, and it gathers into a ball. Picking 'magnets' is a guess. The pull between molecules is electric, but it is not magnetism.

items.p: The pull between a gecko's hair tips and a wall is called a van der Waals force. What kind of force is it, deep down?
opts: An electric pull between atoms that are very close
items.why: When atoms get extremely close, their electric charges shift a little, and they pull on each other weakly. Picking 'gravity' is a common guess, but gravity between a gecko and a wall is far too weak. Experiments ruled out suction.

items.p: Scientists argue about one part of how geckos stick. What is it?
opts: Whether a thin film of water from damp air helps the grip
items.why: Most scientists agree the pull between atoms does most of the work. A 2005 study found gecko hair tips grip harder in damp air, so water may help too. How much each matters is still being studied.

items.p: In 2015, scientists measured air inside termite mounds near Bengaluru. What did they find moves the air?
opts: The walls warming in the day and cooling at night
A fan made of termite wings
items.why: The thin outer walls warm faster than the middle in the day, and cool faster at night. That makes air move one way by day and the other way by night. The old idea was that termites' own warmth pushed air up a chimney.

items.p: The Eastgate Centre in Zimbabwe works exactly like a real termite mound.
items.why: False. It was inspired by termites, but it was based on the old chimney idea of how mounds work, and it also uses fans at night. Scientists later found that real mounds work differently.

items.p: Where do nature's designs, like the burr's hooks, come from?
opts: Evolution: over many generations, living things with features that work better leave more young
A burr thinks hard and plans its hooks
items.why: Burrs with slightly better hooks got carried further, so more of their seeds grew. Their young had good hooks too. Over millions of years the hooks got better. Picking 'the burr plans' is how we often talk, but plants do not plan.

items.p: Which of these is a fact that shows nature's designs are not always perfect?
opts: Your eye has a blind spot, but an octopus eye does not
items.why: Evolution changes what is already there, a little at a time. Our eyes are wired in a way that leaves a blind spot. An octopus eye, which evolved separately, is wired the other way and has none. The other answers show nature's designs working well.

items.p: In 1995, a patent in the USA said using turmeric to heal wounds was a new invention. Why was it cancelled in 1997?
opts: Old Indian books showed people had known it for centuries
Turmeric does not grow in the USA
The inventors forgot to sign it
items.why: A patent is only for something new. India's science council, the CSIR, showed very old writings describing haldi for wounds. So it was not new, and the patent was cancelled.

items.p: A boxfish car was made to copy a fish's shape. Later, scientists found the boxfish's shape mainly helps it to…
opts: Swim very fast in a straight line
items.why: Studies of real boxfish showed their boxy shape helps them turn and steer, more than it helps them swim straight with little drag. The lesson: before copying a shape, find out what it is really for.

items.p: Match each scientist to what they studied.
pairs: A slippery coating copied from the pitcher plant
A book that made the word biomimicry famous
items.why: Barthlott studied the lotus leaf with a powerful microscope. Nakatsu was an engineer and birdwatcher. De Mestral invented Velcro. Aizenberg's team copied the pitcher plant in 2011. Benyus wrote 'Biomimicry' in 1997.

items.p: Animals that are not related ending up with the same shape, because they face the same problem, is called ____ evolution.
items.why: 'Converge' means to come together. Sharks, dolphins and ancient sea reptiles converged on the same streamlined shape.

items.p: With 4 paperclip hooks, a towel held 6 coins. About how many coins would 12 hooks hold, if each hook holds the same?
items.why: 6 coins for 4 hooks. 12 hooks is 3 lots of 4 hooks. 3 times 6 is 18. Picking 12 means matching the coins to the number of hooks, instead of using the pattern. Real results may wobble a little.
items.context: In the fastener challenge, you bent paperclips into hooks, hooked a towel on, and added coins in a bag until it fell.

items.p: Is a bullet train natural or man-made? Give a reason for your answer, and one reason someone might disagree.
items.a: I think it is man-made, because people designed and built it. But someone might say it is natural too, because its nose copies a kingfisher, and people are part of nature.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A good answer gives a reason, and fairly explains another view.

items.p: George de Mestral spent about ten years making Velcro work. A burr took millions of years to evolve its hooks. Who do you think should get the credit for Velcro? Explain.
items.a: I think de Mestral should get the credit for the invention, because he did the work of making it. But the burr should get credit for the idea, because it had the hooks first.
items.why: This is a question about fairness, so any thoughtful answer with a reason is good. You might also think about the weaver who helped him.

items.p: Invent something that copies a living thing you saw this week. Draw it, label the trick you copied, and write how you would test it fairly.
items.a: Any invention with a labelled trick from a real living thing, and a fair test where only one thing changes.
items.why: Inventing means joining a problem, a trick from nature and a fair test. Real engineers do exactly this.

experiments.title: The Leaf That Water Can't Wet
experiments.context: This experiment tests the lotus effect. You drip water on a lotus-like leaf and on other surfaces, tilt them, and see which ones the water rolls off. Then you see if rolling drops can clean away dust.
experiments.question: Which surface makes water roll off in balls? Can rolling drops clean a surface?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the water make round balls, flat puddles or wet patches on the leaf, the steel plate and the paper? Which will stay cleanest when dusty?
experiments.fair_test: Keep everything the same except the surface. Use the same size of drop, from the same spoon or dropper. Tilt every surface to the same height, on the same book. Put 5 drops on each surface, because one drop can be a fluke.
results_table: Drop shape: ball, dome or flat
How many of 5 drops rolled off at the tilt
Did the rolling drops pick up the dust?

materials.item: one water-repelling leaf: an arbi (colocasia) leaf from the vegetable market, a lotus leaf, a nasturtium leaf, or the outer leaf of a cabbage
one ordinary leaf, like a tulsi, money plant or mango leaf
a steel plate and a sheet of paper
a dropper, or a spoon, or a straw (dip it in water and cover the top with your finger)
a small bowl of water
a pinch of chalk dust (rub chalk on rough paper) or a pinch of haldi powder
a thick book, about 3 cm thick, for tilting
a magnifying glass, if you have one

experiments.safety: Haldi stains clothes and fingers yellow. Use chalk dust if you prefer. Wash your hands after touching leaves from outside.

schedule.what: Drip water on four surfaces, tilt them, and do the dust test. Fill in the table.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw what a drop looked like from the side on each surface: a ball, a dome or a flat puddle.

flow.do: 1. Lay the four surfaces flat on a tray or the floor: the water-repelling leaf, the ordinary leaf, the steel plate and the paper. 2. Hold each leaf only by its stalk or its edge. 3. Ask your child to guess what water will do on each.
flow.say: Don't touch the top of the leaves with your fingers. Your fingers can rub off the leaf's secret. What do you think water will do on each one?
flow.kid: Lay out the two leaves, the steel plate and the paper. Hold leaves by the stalk only. Guess: on which one will water roll?
flow.parent: Touching or rubbing the top of a lotus or arbi leaf wipes off its wax. Then that spot gets wet like any leaf. Old, dusty or bruised leaves work less well. Pick a fresh one.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Leaf That Water Can't Wet. You set out a lotus-like leaf and three other surfaces to test with water.

flow.do: 1. Put 5 drops of water on each surface, spaced apart. 2. Crouch down so your eyes are level with the surface. 3. Look at the drops from the side.
flow.say: Get your eyes down low and look at the drops from the side. Are they round like balls, like little domes, or flat?
flow.kid: Put 5 drops on each one. Get your eyes down low. Look from the side. Balls, domes, or flat puddles?

ask.q: What do the drops on the arbi leaf look like?
good: Little silver balls.
Like marbles.
They are round and shiny.

flow.parent: On a good arbi or lotus leaf, the drops look like silver balls or beads of mercury. On steel, they are low domes. On paper, they soak in within a minute. On an ordinary leaf, they spread into flat puddles. On a cabbage leaf, the drops bead up well but are a little flatter than on arbi.

flow.do: 1. Put one end of each surface on the book, so it is tilted. 2. Count how many of the 5 drops roll off. 3. Write the number in the table.
flow.say: Let's tilt each one onto the book. Count: how many of the five drops roll away?
flow.kid: Lift one end of each onto the book. Count how many drops roll off. Write it down.

check.q: On which surface did the drops roll off most easily?
options: The arbi or lotus leaf
The paper
The ordinary leaf
check.why: The arbi or lotus leaf is covered in tiny waxy bumps. A drop sits only on the bump tips, with air under it, so it stays round and rolls at a small tilt. Paper pulls the water in, so it soaks. Picking the ordinary leaf usually means thinking all leaves are the same. Most leaves have no bumps like this, so water spreads on them.

flow.do: 1. Lay the water-repelling leaf and the paper flat again. 2. Sprinkle a thin pinch of chalk dust or haldi on each. 3. Tilt them on the book. 4. Drip drops at the top end, one at a time, and watch them roll down.
flow.say: Now our leaf is dusty, like a lotus in a dirty pond. Watch the drop as it rolls. What happens to the dust?
flow.kid: Sprinkle a little dust on the leaf and the paper. Tilt them. Drip drops at the top. Watch what happens to the dust!

ask.q: What did the rolling drop do on the leaf?
good: It picked up the dust.
It left a clean path behind it.
The dust went into the drop.

flow.think: Did you need to wipe or scrub the leaf? How did it clean itself?
flow.parent: On the leaf, each rolling drop gathers the dust and leaves a clean stripe behind. Look with the magnifying glass if you have one. On the paper, the water soaks in and the dust becomes a wet smudge. If drops stick on your leaf, try a fresher leaf, or a spot you have not touched.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Let's finish like real scientists. Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Finish like a scientist. Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: the arbi leaf keeps itself clean. What I saw: all 5 drops rolled off it, and they picked up the chalk dust. On paper, no drops rolled and the dust made a smudge. Why: the leaf has tiny waxy bumps, so water makes balls that roll and carry dirt away.
